pos: n. (a full remission of the temporal punishment due to sin, granted by the church out of the treasury of merit, for a pilgrimage, a crusade, a gift or a prescribed devotion)
etymology: Latin indulgentia plenaria, from plenus, full, and indulgere, to be lenient — a complete remission.
biblical_def: A plenary indulgence is a full remission of the temporal penalty of sin, as distinguished from a partial one measured in days or years. It rests on a structure of doctrine: that sin's guilt is forgiven in absolution but a temporal penalty remains, to be worked off in this life or in purgatory, and that the church may remit it from a treasury accumulated by the merits of Christ and the saints. Plenary indulgences were attached to the First Crusade, to jubilee pilgrimages to Rome, and from 1476 could be applied to the dead — which is the point at which the preaching of them in Germany produced Luther's theses. The objection is not merely to the abuse. Scripture knows no remainder to be worked off: “Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom 3:24). The word freely there renders a Greek adverb meaning gratuitously, with no cause in the receiver, and Paul closes the door on any supplement: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8), “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines indulgence as, in the Romish church, remission of the punishment due to sins granted by the pope; and plenary as full, entire, complete.
webster_full: INDULGENCE, n. In the Romish church, remission of the punishment due to sins, granted by the pope or church, and supposed to save the sinner from purgatory.
PLENARY, a. Full; entire; complete; as a plenary indulgence.
REMISSION, n. The act of remitting, sending back. Forgiveness; pardon; that is, the giving up of the punishment due to a crime.
MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward.
PURGATORY, n. Among catholics, a supposed place or state after death, in which the souls of persons are purified, or in which they expiate such offenses as do not merit eternal damnation.
scriptures: Rom 3:24
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
corruption_summary: A full remission of sin's temporal penalty, drawn on a treasury of merit, and the gospel that knows no remainder.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a treasury. The whole apparatus requires a surplus of merit belonging to someone other than Christ and administrable by an office, and once such a stock exists it will be distributed on terms — a crusade, a jubilee, a gift to a building fund. The sale that outraged Luther was a symptom; the ledger was the disease. Isaiah's invitation is constructed to exclude any such terms: “he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isa 55:1).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the completeness of justification, which is a verdict and not a process with a balance outstanding. “Being justified freely by his grace” (Rom 3:24) uses a courtroom word, and a man acquitted does not serve a reduced sentence. The reason Paul gives for excluding works is pastoral as well as doctrinal: “lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9).
roots_summary: Latin indulgentia plenaria, full remission; Greek dorean (G1432), freely, as a gift; Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify; Greek charis (G5485), grace; Greek doron (G1435), a gift.
roots_lines: Latin indulgere — to be lenient, to grant; whence indulgence.
Greek dorean (G1432) — freely, without cause or payment; “justified freely by his grace” (Rom 3:24).
Greek apolutrosis (G629) — redemption by ransom; “through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom 3:24).
Greek charis (G5485) — grace, unmerited favour; “For by grace are ye saved through faith” (Eph 2:8).
Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to boast; “lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9).
usage: “and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) — the clause a treasury contradicts.
“without money and without price” (Isa 55:1) — the terms, which are none.
“Being justified freely” (Rom 3:24) — a verdict, not an instalment plan.

pos: n. (a man licensed to preach indulgences and collect the offerings attached to them; by the fourteenth century a byword for fraud)
etymology: Anglo-French pardoner, from pardoner, to pardon, from Latin perdonare, to remit entirely — one who carries pardons.
biblical_def: A pardoner, or quaestor, travelled with a licence, a sheaf of papal letters and often a bag of relics, preached in parish churches, and collected offerings for the indulgence he carried. Many were frauds outright; the Council of Vienne in 1312 and the Council of Trent both legislated against them, and Trent finally abolished the office. Chaucer's Pardoner, who preaches brilliantly against avarice in order to make money and knows exactly what he is, remains the sharpest portrait in English, and he is drawn by a man writing inside the church rather than against it. The pardoner is therefore not a Protestant invention: the office was condemned by the authority that licensed it, and continued because the revenue was wanted. Peter had described the type before there were any: “through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you: whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not” (2Pe 2:3). Paul's instruction to Titus about such men is blunt about both the remedy and the motive: “Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake” (Tit 1:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pardoner as one who forgives, and formerly one who sold indulgences; and merchandise as the objects of commerce, and the act of trading.
webster_full: PARDONER, n. One who pardons or forgives. Formerly, one who sold or carried about indulgences.
MERCHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities, whatever is usually bought or sold in trade. Trade; traffic; commerce.
QUESTOR, n. In Roman antiquity, a treasurer. In the church, one licensed to collect alms or offerings.
AVARICE, n. An inordinate desire of gaining and possessing wealth; covetousness; greediness or insatiable desire of gain.
IMPOSTOR, n. One who imposes on others; a person who assumes a character for the purpose of deception.
scriptures: And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you: whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not.
Tit 1:11
Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Act 8:20
But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.
corruption_summary: The licensed seller of pardons, a byword for fraud two centuries before the Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the gospel with a price list, and the most damning thing about the pardoners is that the church knew. Councils condemned them, bishops restricted them, satirists mocked them, and the system kept them because the money was needed. Peter's phrase for the method is exact: “with feigned words make merchandise of you” (2Pe 2:3) — the words are the product, and the congregation is the commodity.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the motive test Peter applies to every minister: “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). It is not enough that the doctrine preached be sound; the reason for preaching it is itself under judgement. Peter's word to Simon of Samaria settles the question of whether God's gifts may ever enter a market: “Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money” (Act 8:20).
roots_summary: Latin perdonare, to remit; Greek pleonexia (G4124), covetousness; Greek emporeuomai (G1710), to make merchandise of; Greek plastos (G4112), feigned or moulded; Greek aischrokerdos (G147), for filthy gain.
roots_lines: Latin perdonare — to remit entirely; whence pardon and pardoner.
Greek pleonexia (G4124) — greed, covetousness; “through covetousness” (2Pe 2:3).
Greek emporeuomai (G1710) — to trade in, to make merchandise of; “make merchandise of you” (2Pe 2:3).
Greek plastos (G4112) — moulded, fabricated; “with feigned words” (2Pe 2:3).
Greek aischrokerdos (G147) — from a base love of gain; “not for filthy lucre” (1Pe 5:2).
usage: “their damnation slumbereth not” (2Pe 2:3) — said of men who were not yet born.
“Whose mouths must be stopped” (Tit 1:11) — the remedy, which is not debate.
“Thy money perish with thee” (Act 8:20) — the gift is not for sale.

pos: n. (a cheap lead or pewter token sold at a shrine and worn openly, proving that a pilgrim had made the journey — the scallop of Compostela, the ampulla of Canterbury)
etymology: From pilgrim, Latin peregrinus, a foreigner, and badge, of uncertain origin — a mark worn to be seen.
biblical_def: Pilgrim badges were mass-produced at every major shrine and sold by the thousand: the scallop shell of Santiago, the little ampulla of Canterbury water said to be mixed with Becket's blood, the keys of Rome, the Virgin's image at Walsingham. They were pinned to hat or cloak, and they certified the journey to anyone who saw them. Thousands have been dredged from the Thames, thrown in on the pilgrim's return. As an object they are entirely innocent; as a practice they are the exact thing our Lord censured in another religious badge: “all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments” (Mat 23:5). The Christian's own mark is not worn and cannot be bought: “in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise” (Eph 1:13), and “Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts” (2Co 1:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines badge as a mark, sign, token or thing by which a person is distinguished; and token as a sign, something intended to represent or indicate another thing or event.
webster_full: BADGE, n. A mark, sign, token or thing by which a person is distinguished, in a particular place or employment, and designating his relation to a person or to a particular occupation.
TOKEN, n. A sign; something intended to represent or indicate another thing or an event.
SEAL, n. A piece of metal or other hard substance on which is engraved some image or device, used to make an impression. That which confirms, ratifies or makes stable.
EARNEST, n. First fruits; that which is in advance, and gives promise of something to come. A pledge; a part paid beforehand as a security for the whole.
AMPULLA, n. A small flask or vessel for holding liquids; in the church, a vessel for holy oil or water.
scriptures: Mat 6:1
Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.
Eph 1:13
In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise,
Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts.
Eph 4:30
And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.
corruption_summary: The lead token proving a pilgrimage, worn where everyone could see it, and the seal that no one can.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is certified devotion. A badge exists to be read by other people, and once piety can be evidenced it will be collected. Our Lord's objection to the broad phylactery was not that the parchment was wrong but that the breadth was for an audience, and he states the principle before he gives any examples: “Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 6:1).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer already has a mark, and it is internal, unforgeable and given rather than earned. “and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts” (2Co 1:22) makes the Spirit himself the down payment on what is coming. The warning attached is about grieving rather than losing him: “grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption” (Eph 4:30).
roots_summary: Latin peregrinus, a foreigner; Greek sphragizo (G4972), to seal; Greek arrabon (G728), a pledge or earnest; Greek phulakterion (G5440), a phylactery; Greek theaomai (G2300), to be gazed at.
roots_lines: Latin peregrinus — a foreigner, a traveller; whence pilgrim.
Greek theaomai (G2300) — to behold, to be seen; “to be seen of them” (Mat 6:1).
Greek sphragizo (G4972) — to seal, to mark as one's own; “ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise” (Eph 1:13).
Greek arrabon (G728) — a down payment, an earnest; “and given the earnest of the Spirit” (2Co 1:22).
Greek lupeo (G3076) — to grieve, to make sorrowful; “And grieve not the holy Spirit of God” (Eph 4:30).
usage: “they make broad their phylacteries” (Mat 23:5) — the badge, in its first century form.
“ye have no reward of your Father” (Mat 6:1) — the cost of a visible piety.
“sealed with that holy Spirit of promise” (Eph 1:13) — the mark nobody can see.

pos: n. (the privilege by which a man in orders, and later any man who could read, escaped the secular court's sentence for felony and was handed to the church courts)
etymology: Medieval Latin privilegium clericale, the clerical privilege; the English phrase is from the plea benefit of clergy entered after conviction.
biblical_def: Benefit of clergy began as the claim that a clerk accused of felony must be tried by the church and not hanged by the king, and it was the immediate cause of Becket's quarrel with Henry II. Because literacy proved clerical status, the test became the reading of a verse, and because the verse chosen was almost always the same one it got a name: the neck-verse, Psalm 51 verse 1, “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness” (Psa 51:1). By the sixteenth century any man who could read, or who had memorised that line, escaped the gallows once. The irony is total: a psalm of genuine penitence recited as a password by men who were often neither penitent nor literate, while an illiterate man beside them hanged. God's own courts allow no such distinction: “For there is no respect of persons with God” (Rom 2:11), and the law of Israel bound the judge to the same rule: “thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty” (Lev 19:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines benefit of clergy as an exemption of the persons of clergymen from criminal process before a secular judge; and partiality as inclination to favor one party or one side of a question more than the other.
webster_full: BENEFIT OF CLERGY, n. In English law, an exemption of the persons of clergymen from criminal process before a secular judge; a privilege afterwards extended to all who could read.
PARTIALITY, n. Inclination to favor one party or one side of a question more than the other; an undue bias of mind.
FELONY, n. Any crime which incurs the forfeiture of lands or goods; a capital offense.
PRIVILEGE, n. A particular and peculiar benefit or advantage enjoyed by a person, company or society, beyond the common advantages of other citizens.
CONTRITE, a. Literally, worn or bruised. Hence, broken-hearted for sin; deeply affected with grief and sorrow for having offended God.
scriptures: Psa 51:1

To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.
Rom 2:11
For there is no respect of persons with God.
Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
corruption_summary: The neck-verse: Psalm 51 recited as a password by men escaping the gallows, while the illiterate hanged.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the use of Scripture as a formula. A verse whose whole content is a plea of guilt and a cry for mercy became the means by which guilty men avoided the consequence of their guilt, recited by rote and tested by a bishop's clerk. That the words were the right words made it worse, not better. And the inequality was the point: literacy was wealth, so the privilege was a class privilege wearing a cassock.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the psalm actually asks for, which is not escape: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Psa 51:17). David wrote it after a murder and did not ask to be spared the consequences. The impartiality of God's judgement is the other half, and it cuts both ways — “thou shalt not respect the person of the poor” (Lev 19:15) forbids the fashionable injustice as well as the old one.
roots_summary: Latin privilegium clericale, the clerk's privilege; Hebrew chanan (H2603), to be gracious; Greek prosopolepsia (G4382), respect of persons; Hebrew panim (H6440), the face or person; Hebrew dakah (H1794), to crush or break.
roots_lines: Latin privilegium clericale — the clerical privilege, pleaded after conviction.
Hebrew chanan (H2603) — to show favour; “Have mercy upon me, O God” (Psa 51:1).
Greek prosopolepsia (G4382) — partiality, respect of persons; “no respect of persons with God” (Rom 2:11).
Hebrew panim (H6440) — the face; the idiom behind respecting a person; “nor honour the person of the mighty” (Lev 19:15).
Hebrew dakah (H1794) — to crush, to break in pieces; “a broken and a contrite heart” (Psa 51:17).
usage: “according to thy lovingkindness” (Psa 51:1) — the neck-verse, read as a password.
“thou wilt not despise” (Psa 51:17) — what the psalm actually asks.
“For there is no respect of persons with God” (Rom 2:11) — no benefit of clergy there.

pos: n. (the privilege by which a fugitive who reached a church was immune from arrest for forty days, after which he confessed his crime and abjured the realm)
etymology: From sanctuary, Latin sanctuarium, a holy place; the English right was codified in Anglo-Saxon law and abolished for crime in 1623.
biblical_def: A fugitive who reached a parish church in medieval England, grasped the knocker or sat in the frith-stool, was safe from arrest for forty days. He could then confess before the coroner, forswear the kingdom, and walk to a named port carrying a cross, after which he was outlaw if he returned. Certain great churches — Durham, Beverley, Westminster — claimed wider and permanent sanctuary. The institution derives from the cities of refuge, which were not immunity but a guarantee of trial: “they shall be unto you cities for refuge from the avenger; that the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment” (Num 35:12). The limit of the altar's protection is given once and decisively. Joab fled and “caught hold on the horns of the altar” (1Ki 2:28), and refused to come out, saying “Nay; but I will die here” (1Ki 2:30). Solomon's order is the whole doctrine: the altar does not shelter blood guilt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sanctuary as a place of protection, a sacred asylum, and the holiest part of the temple; and asylum as a sanctuary or place of refuge where criminals and debtors shelter themselves from justice.
webster_full: SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple. Hence, a place of protection; a sacred asylum.
ASYLUM, n. A sanctuary or place of refuge, where criminals and debtors shelter themselves from justice, and from which they cannot be taken without sacrilege.
ABJURE, v.t. To renounce upon oath; to abandon; as, to abjure the realm, which is to swear to leave the country and never to return.
AVENGER, n. One who avenges or vindicates; a vindicator; a revenger.
OUTLAW, n. A person excluded from the benefit of the law, or deprived of its protection.
scriptures: And they shall be unto you cities for refuge from the avenger; that the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment.
Then tidings came to Joab: for Joab had turned after Adonijah, though he turned not after Absalom. And Joab fled unto the tabernacle of the LORD, and caught hold on the horns of the altar.

And Benaiah came to the tabernacle of the LORD, and said unto him, Thus saith the king, Come forth. And he said, Nay; but I will die here. And Benaiah brought the king word again, saying, Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me.
And the king said unto him, Do as he hath said, and fall upon him, and bury him; that thou mayest take away the innocent blood, which Joab shed, from me, and from the house of my father.
corruption_summary: Forty days' immunity in a church, and the one man in Scripture who held the altar and was killed at it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is immunity mistaken for refuge. The cities of refuge existed so that a man who had killed at unawares should not be cut down by an avenger before a court heard him; they protected the process, not the guilty. Medieval sanctuary drifted into a general suspension of justice, and the great sanctuaries became districts full of men who had no intention of standing trial anywhere.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Solomon's ruling, which no one who appeals to sanctuary should be allowed to forget: “Do as he hath said, and fall upon him, and bury him; that thou mayest take away the innocent blood, which Joab shed” (1Ki 2:31). The altar was not built to defeat justice, and a church that offers shelter to the unconvicted is doing one thing while a church that offers escape to the convicted is doing another.
roots_summary: Latin sanctuarium, a holy place; Hebrew miqlat (H4733), a refuge; Hebrew goel (H1350), an avenger or kinsman-redeemer; Hebrew qeren (H7161), a horn; Hebrew dam naqi, innocent blood.
roots_lines: Latin sanctuarium — a holy place; the English right was codified before the Conquest.
Hebrew miqlat (H4733) — a refuge, an asylum; “cities for refuge from the avenger” (Num 35:12).
Hebrew goel (H1350) — the avenger of blood, the near kinsman.
Hebrew qeren (H7161) — a horn; “caught hold on the horns of the altar” (1Ki 2:28).
Hebrew naqi (H5355) — innocent, clean; “take away the innocent blood” (1Ki 2:31).
usage: “until he stand before the congregation in judgment” (Num 35:12) — refuge guarantees a trial.
“Nay; but I will die here” (1Ki 2:30) — and he did.
“which Joab shed” (1Ki 2:31) — the altar does not cover blood guilt.

pos: n. (a parish festival at which ale brewed from donated malt was sold to raise money for the church, held at Whitsun and other seasons; suppressed by Puritan magistrates in the seventeenth century)
etymology: Old English ealu, ale, used of the drink and then of the feast at which it was drunk — as in bride-ale, whence bridal.
biblical_def: A church ale was a parish fundraiser. Parishioners gave malt, the churchwardens brewed, and the whole village bought and drank in the church house or sometimes the nave itself, with games, dancing and a lord of the ale presiding. The accounts of many English parishes show the roof and the bells paid for this way. In the later sixteenth and seventeenth centuries Puritan magistrates in the west country suppressed them, and the quarrel over whether they should be allowed became a national one under Charles I. Both sides had a text. The law of Israel positively commands a feast with strong drink at the central sanctuary: “thou shalt bestow that money for whatsoever thy soul lusteth after, for oxen, or for sheep, or for wine, or for strong drink” (Deu 14:26), and the purpose named is joy before God. Against it stands the apostolic reminder that “the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost” (Rom 14:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ale as a liquor made from an infusion of malt by fermentation, and also a merry meeting in English country places; and revel as a feast with loose and noisy jollity.
webster_full: ALE, n. A liquor made from an infusion of malt by fermentation. In England, also, a merry meeting in English country places, so called from the liquor drunk.
REVEL, n. A feast with loose and noisy jollity.
CHURCHWARDEN, n. A keeper or guardian of the church, and a representative of the parish.
WHITSUNTIDE, n. The season of Pentecost; so called, it is supposed, from the white garments formerly worn by those newly baptized.
TEMPERANCE, n. Moderation; particularly, habitual moderation in regard to the indulgence of the natural appetites and passions.
scriptures: And thou shalt bestow that money for whatsoever thy soul lusteth after, for oxen, or for sheep, or for wine, or for strong drink, or for whatsoever thy soul desireth: and thou shalt eat there before the LORD thy God, and thou shalt rejoice, thou, and thine household,
For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.
Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
corruption_summary: The parish ale that paid for the church roof, and the quarrel between two texts about it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is real on both sides and this dictionary will say so. A fundraiser that leaves half a parish drunk in the churchyard is not sanctified by its purpose, and Paul's command is not negotiable: “be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18). Equally, a piety that cannot distinguish drunkenness from drink has added to Scripture, and Deuteronomy 14 is sitting there with strong drink in it, commanded.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Bible condemns drunkenness absolutely and prohibits drink nowhere, and that a conscience bound beyond Scripture is bound by men. The governing rule covers the ale and the magistrate who suppressed it alike: “Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God” (1Co 10:31). Everything then turns on whether the glory of God is actually the aim, which the parish accounts cannot settle either way.
roots_summary: Old English ealu, ale; Hebrew shekar (H7941), strong drink; Hebrew samach (H8055), to rejoice; Greek asotia (G810), excess or riot; Greek doxa (G1391), glory.
roots_lines: Old English ealu — ale; and the feast named from it, as in bride-ale.
Hebrew shekar (H7941) — strong drink; “or for wine, or for strong drink” (Deu 14:26).
Hebrew samach (H8055) — to rejoice, to be glad; “and thou shalt rejoice, thou, and thine household” (Deu 14:26).
Greek asotia (G810) — riot, dissoluteness; “wherein is excess” (Eph 5:18).
Greek doxa (G1391) — glory; “do all to the glory of God” (1Co 10:31).
usage: “and thou shalt eat there before the LORD thy God” (Deu 14:26) — a commanded feast.
“be not drunk with wine” (Eph 5:18) — the absolute prohibition, which is of drunkenness.
“but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost” (Rom 14:17) — the kingdom is not the quarrel.

pos: n. (the suppression of all religious houses in England, Wales and Ireland between 1536 and 1541, and the transfer of their lands to the crown)
etymology: From Latin dissolutio, a loosing apart, from dissolvere, to unbind; the technical term in the surrender deeds.
biblical_def: Between 1536 and 1541 every religious house in England, Wales and Ireland was suppressed: about eight hundred communities, some ten thousand religious, and property worth perhaps a fifth of the kingdom's landed wealth. The lesser houses went by statute in 1536, the greater by surrender and attainder thereafter, and the lands were sold within a generation to a gentry who would never permit their return. A Reformed dictionary must say two things at once and resist the temptation to say only one. The doctrinal case against the houses was substantially sound: masses for the dead, relic shrines, purchased merit. The confidence of their defenders was also the confidence Jeremiah demolished: “Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these” (Jer 7:4). And our Lord's word over a greater building settles what buildings are worth: “There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dissolution as the act of liberating or breaking up, the separation of the parts of a body; and suppression as the act of putting down, destroying or concealing.
webster_full: DISSOLUTION, n. The act of liberating or breaking up. The separation of the parts of a body which destroys its form.
SUPPRESSION, n. The act of suppressing, crushing or destroying. The act of concealing; a keeping secret.
SURRENDER, n. The act of yielding or resigning one's person or the possession of something into the power of another.
ATTAINDER, n. Literally a staining, corruption or rendering impure; a corruption of blood. The judgment of death, or sentence of a competent tribunal upon a person convicted of treason or felony.
SACRILEGE, n. The crime of violating or profaning sacred things, or of alienating to common purposes what has been consecrated to religious uses.
scriptures: Jer 7:4
Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these.
Mat 24:2
And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.
Jer 7:11
Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, even I have seen it, saith the LORD.
Mic 2:2
And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage.
corruption_summary: Eight hundred houses suppressed in five years, a sound doctrinal case, and a transfer of a fifth of England to courtiers.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is on both sides of the account, and the Protestant half must be stated plainly. Jeremiah's charge against the temple establishment applies to the houses: “Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?” (Jer 7:11). But the men who dissolved them were not reformers acting on a doctrine of the church; they were a king who needed money and courtiers who wanted land, and Micah's description fits them exactly — “they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away” (Mic 2:2).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a right judgement may be executed by the wrong hands for the wrong reasons, and that God is not thereby implicated in the motives. Nothing in Scripture suggests that the removal of an idolatrous institution sanctifies the men who profited; Assyria was the rod of God's anger and was judged for the swing. “See ye not all these things?” (Mat 24:2) was said about a temple God himself had commanded.
roots_summary: Latin dissolvere, to unbind; Hebrew sheqer (H8267), falsehood; Hebrew meharah, a den; Greek kataluo (G2647), to throw down; Hebrew gazal (H1497), to seize.
roots_lines: Latin dissolutio — a loosing apart; the word in the surrender deeds.
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, a lie; “Trust ye not in lying words” (Jer 7:4).
Hebrew parits (H6530) — a robber, a violent one; “become a den of robbers in your eyes” (Jer 7:11).
Greek kataluo (G2647) — to loosen down, to destroy; “that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2).
Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, to take by force; “and take them by violence” (Mic 2:2).
usage: “The temple of the LORD, are these” (Jer 7:4) — the defenders' confidence, demolished.
“a den of robbers” (Jer 7:11) — the charge against the houses.
“and houses, and take them away” (Mic 2:2) — the charge against the dissolvers.

pos: n. (the survey of the income of every ecclesiastical benefice and religious house in England and Wales, made in 1535 on the king's commission)
etymology: Latin valor ecclesiasticus, the church valuation, from valere, to be worth — the worth of the church, reckoned in pounds.
biblical_def: The Valor Ecclesiasticus is the greatest single record of the pre-Reformation English church: commissioners in every county returned the gross and net income of every benefice, chantry, hospital and religious house, parish by parish, in 1535. Its immediate purpose was fiscal, since the crown had just annexed the clerical first fruits and tenth; its real purpose became apparent when the suppression statute of 1536 used its figures to define the lesser houses that would go. It remains the historian's indispensable source, and it was also an act of counting performed immediately before a seizure. The commissioners were local gentry, many of whom would shortly be buying what they had just valued, and the returns were taken on oath from the houses themselves, which had every reason to understate and little opportunity to do so. A survey is never a neutral instrument; it is made by someone, for something. Scripture records one famous numbering and does not treat it as neutral administration: “Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel” (1Ch 21:1), and the verdict is flat — “God was displeased with this thing; therefore he smote Israel” (1Ch 21:7). The census itself was not forbidden; what it expressed was.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines valuation as the act of valuing, appraisement, estimated worth; and survey as a particular view, an examination of all the parts or particulars of a thing.
webster_full: VALUATION, n. The act of valuing; appraisement; a setting of the value. Value set upon a thing; appraised worth.
SURVEY, n. A particular view; an examination of all the parts or particulars of a thing, with a design to ascertain the condition, quantity or quality.
FIRST FRUITS, n. In the church of England, the profits of every spiritual benefice for the first year.
TENTH, n. In England, the tenth part of the annual profit of every living, formerly paid to the pope, afterwards to the king.
COMMISSIONER, n. A person who has a commission or warrant to perform some office, or execute some business, for the person or government which employs him.
scriptures: And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel.
And God was displeased with this thing; therefore he smote Israel.
And David said unto God, I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing: but now, I beseech thee, do away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly.

When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the LORD, when thou numberest them; that there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them.
corruption_summary: The 1535 survey of every church income in England, which the suppression statute then used to pick its targets.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is not the counting but the appetite the counting serves. Numbering Israel was lawful when God commanded it and fatal when David wanted it, and the difference lay entirely in why. A survey of what the church owns, made by a government that is about to take it, is a different act from a survey made by a steward. David's own verdict on himself is the honest one: “I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing: but now, I beseech thee, do away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly” (1Ch 21:8).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the law had provided for a census and attached a ransom to it, precisely so that counting should not become possessing: “When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the LORD, when thou numberest them; that there be no plague among them” (Exo 30:12). A people counted belongs to God, and the counter must pay to be reminded of it.
roots_summary: Latin valor ecclesiasticus, the church valuation; Hebrew manah (H4487), to count; Hebrew saphar (H5608), to number; Hebrew kopher (H3724), a ransom; Hebrew negeph (H5063), a plague.
roots_lines: Latin valere — to be worth; the survey's title says only how much the church is worth.
Hebrew manah (H4487) — to count, to appoint; “provoked David to number Israel” (1Ch 21:1).
Hebrew nagaph (H5062) — to smite; “therefore he smote Israel” (1Ch 21:7).
Hebrew kopher (H3724) — a ransom, a covering price; “a ransom for his soul unto the LORD” (Exo 30:12).
Hebrew negeph (H5063) — a plague, a blow; “that there be no plague among them” (Exo 30:12).
usage: “And God was displeased with this thing” (1Ch 21:7) — a census is never merely arithmetic.
“I have done very foolishly” (1Ch 21:8) — the counter's own verdict.
“when thou numberest them” (Exo 30:12) — counting with a ransom attached.

pos: n. (the English court of record erected in 1536 to administer, lease and sell the monastic lands taken by the crown, and to pay pensions to the dispossessed)
etymology: From its full title, the Court of the Augmentations of the Revenues of the King's Crown — Latin augmentatio, an increase.
biblical_def: The Court of Augmentations was the administrative machine of the dissolution: a chancellor, a treasurer, auditors and receivers in every county, erected in 1536 to take in the surrendered houses, value their lands, lease them, sell them and pay the pensions of the dispossessed religious. It did its work with efficiency and a good deal of honesty — the pensions were largely paid — and within fifteen years most of the land had passed to purchasers. The crown spent the proceeds on war with France and Scotland and was nearly as poor at the end as at the beginning. Its name is its own commentary: a court for the increase of the king's revenues. Habakkuk supplies the proverb for such an office: “Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay!” (Hab 2:6). The image of a man loading himself with the heavy mud he has scraped up is deliberate, and it is a picture of a treasury.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines augmentation as the act of increasing or making larger, the state of being increased; and exchequer as the court or office in England in which the revenues of the crown are received.
webster_full: AUGMENTATION, n. The act of increasing or making larger, by addition, expansion or dilatation. The state of being increased or enlarged.
EXCHEQUER, n. In England, an ancient court of record, intended principally to collect and superintend the king's debts and duties.
ESCHEAT, n. The falling of lands or tenements to the lord of the fee, for want of heirs or by forfeiture.
PENSION, n. An annual allowance of a sum of money to a person by government, for past services.
SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; particularly in war, the plunder taken from an enemy.
scriptures: Hab 2:6

Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay!
Hab 2:9
Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil!
Isa 10:6

I will send him against an hypocritical nation, and against the people of my wrath will I give him a charge, to take the spoil, and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets.
Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase.
corruption_summary: The court that sold England's monastic lands in fifteen years, named for the increase of the king's revenues.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is plunder conducted with excellent paperwork. The Court of Augmentations was not corrupt in the ordinary sense; it kept its books, paid its pensions and gave value. What it did was transfer, in a decade and a half, the endowment of English religion into private hands by the mechanism of a sale. Habakkuk's woe names the motive beneath such orderly acquisition: “Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil!” (Hab 2:9).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the proverb about how such gains behave: “Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase” (Pro 13:11). Henry VIII took a fifth of the land of England and died needing money. Isaiah's word to the instrument of judgement applies to the whole episode — the nation sent “to take the spoil, and to take the prey” (Isa 10:6) was itself under sentence for the way it did it.
roots_summary: Latin augmentatio, an increase; Hebrew rabah (H7235), to multiply; Hebrew betsa (H1215), unjust gain; Hebrew shalal (H7998), spoil; Hebrew hebel (H1892), vanity or vapour.
roots_lines: Latin augmentatio — an increase; the court's own name for its business.
Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to increase, to multiply; “Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his!” (Hab 2:6).
Hebrew betsa (H1215) — gain made by violence; “that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house” (Hab 2:9).
Hebrew shalal (H7998) — spoil, plunder; “to take the spoil, and to take the prey” (Isa 10:6).
Hebrew hebel (H1892) — vapour, vanity; “Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished” (Pro 13:11).
usage: “and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay!” (Hab 2:6) — the picture of a treasury.
“that he may set his nest on high” (Hab 2:9) — the motive of orderly plunder.
“but he that gathereth by labour shall increase” (Pro 13:11) — the contrast, and the outcome.

pos: n. (the rising in the north of England in 1536 against the dissolution of the monasteries and the religious policy of the crown, dispersed on a promise of pardon and a parliament, and then punished by execution)
etymology: The name the insurgents gave themselves — a pilgrimage rather than a rebellion, marching under the banner of the Five Wounds.
biblical_def: In October 1536 the commons of Lincolnshire and then of Yorkshire rose in the largest rebellion any Tudor faced: perhaps thirty thousand men under Robert Aske, a lawyer, marching under the banner of the Five Wounds and calling themselves pilgrims, demanding the restoration of the suppressed houses and the removal of the king's ministers. The duke of Norfolk, badly outnumbered, negotiated. A free pardon and a parliament at York were promised in the king's name, the host dispersed on that promise, and when a separate rising broke out in 1537 the promise was treated as void. Aske, who had worked to keep the peace, was hanged in chains at York. Ezekiel pronounced on a king who broke a sworn word: “Seeing he despised the oath by breaking the covenant, when, lo, he had given his hand, and hath done all these things, he shall not escape” (Eze 17:18), and God claims the broken oath as his own: “mine oath that he hath despised, and my covenant that he hath broken, even it will I recompense upon his own head” (Eze 17:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines insurrection as a rising against civil or political authority, the open and active opposition of a number of persons to the execution of a law; and pardon as forgiveness, the remission of a penalty.
webster_full: INSURRECTION, n. A rising against civil or political authority; the open and active opposition of a number of persons to the execution of a law in a city or state.
PARDON, n. Forgiveness; the remission of a penalty; the release of an obligation or a penalty.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable.
TRUCE, n. A suspension of arms by agreement of the commanders of opposing armies; a temporary cessation of hostilities.
PERFIDY, n. The act of violating faith, a promise, vow or allegiance; treachery.
scriptures: Seeing he despised the oath by breaking the covenant, when, lo, he had given his hand, and hath done all these things, he shall not escape.
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; As I live, surely mine oath that he hath despised, and my covenant that he hath broken, even it will I recompense upon his own head.
Jos 9:19
But all the princes said unto all the congregation, We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel: now therefore we may not touch them.
Psa 15:4
In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
corruption_summary: Thirty thousand northern men dispersed on a king's promise of pardon, and the promise broken within a year.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the oath kept only while it is convenient. A reader of this dictionary will not share the pilgrims' religion; their demands included the restoration of houses whose doctrine Scripture condemns, and the dictionary says so elsewhere without softening it. That is beside the point here. A pardon was sworn in the king's name to men who laid down their arms on the strength of it, and Ezekiel says of a man who did the same thing that “he shall not escape” (Eze 17:18).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an oath binds even when it was obtained under pressure and even when the other party does not deserve it. Israel swore to the Gibeonites under deception and kept the oath anyway: “We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel: now therefore we may not touch them” (Jos 9:19). The man God receives is the one who “sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” (Psa 15:4), and a king is not exempt from the psalm.
roots_summary: Hebrew alah (H423), an oath or curse; Hebrew berith (H1285), a covenant; Hebrew bazah (H959), to despise; Hebrew shaba (H7650), to swear; Hebrew nathan yad, to give the hand.
roots_lines: The insurgents' own word: a pilgrimage, not a rebellion, under the banner of the Five Wounds.
Hebrew alah (H423) — an oath, a sworn curse; “he despised the oath by breaking the covenant” (Eze 17:18).
Hebrew bazah (H959) — to despise, to hold in contempt; “mine oath that he hath despised” (Eze 17:19).
Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant; “and my covenant that he hath broken” (Eze 17:19).
Hebrew shaba (H7650) — to swear, to bind by oath; “We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel” (Jos 9:19).
usage: “when, lo, he had given his hand” (Eze 17:18) — the handshake counted as the oath.
“now therefore we may not touch them” (Jos 9:19) — an oath kept though obtained by fraud.
“and changeth not” (Psa 15:4) — the standard a king is not exempt from.
